Think about what must be happening to the muscle wall of the atria to push blood down through the open atrioventricular valves.
walkthrough:
Read the Blood Flow Arrows**
In both diagrams the arrows show blood moving downwards from the upper chambers into the lower chambers. The upper chambers are the atria and the lower chambers are the ventricles. So blood is moving from atria to ventricles through the atrioventricular valves.

Link Chamber Size to Contraction**
Muscle chambers get smaller in volume when they contract because the wall squeezes in on the blood. In Stage B the atrial walls look much thinner and smaller than in Stage A, while the ventricles are still relaxed and filling. Contraction of the atria pushing blood into the ventricles is atrial systole.

Final answer: stage B is atrial systole (atrial contraction); evidence: atria are smaller than in A and atrioventricular (bicuspid and tricuspid) valves are open with blood flowing from atria into ventricles.

hints: Start where blood leaves the heart - trace the outlet from each ventricle into the large artery above it and focus on the junction between ventricle and artery.
walkthrough:
Locate the Two Exit Doors**
There are two types of valves in the heart. The atrioventricular valves are in the middle of the heart between atria and ventricles. The semilunar valves are higher up, at the very base of the two great arteries leaving the ventricles - the pulmonary artery from the right ventricle and the aorta from the left ventricle.

Place the Label**
A line drawn to either of those two junctions, just inside the start of the artery, correctly identifies a semilunar valve. They are closed in Fig. 6.1 because blood is not being ejected into the arteries at this stage.
Final answer: Label line S to the base of the aorta or the base of the pulmonary artery, at the junction between ventricle and artery where the semilunar valve sits.

hints: Think about what happens to pressure in the ventricles when they relax after pumping blood out into the aorta and pulmonary artery.
Think about which direction blood would tend to fall back under gravity and higher arterial pressure, and what structure must stop it.
walkthrough:
Why Backflow Is a Risk**
During ventricular systole the ventricles contract and push blood up through the open semilunar valves into the aorta and pulmonary artery. When the ventricles then relax, pressure in the ventricles falls below pressure in the arteries, so blood would tend to flow backwards.

How the Valves Ensure One-Way Flow**
The semilunar valves snap shut as blood starts to fall back, the cusps filling like little pockets. This blocks the opening and keeps blood in the arteries moving away from the heart, so flow is always ventricles to arteries and never reversed.
Final answer: Prevent backflow of blood from the aorta and pulmonary artery into the ventricles, ensuring one-way flow from ventricles to arteries.
